conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is well-supported by evidence, stating clearly that hands-only CPR clearly improves survival compared to no bystander CPR.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The evidence does not support the claim that hands-only CPR is false—it is well supported. Multiple large studies and meta-analyses consistently show that bystander CPR (whether hands-only/compression-only or conventional with rescue breaths) improves survival compared with no bystander CPR at all, in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).

Key evidence:
- The American Heart Association's science advisory concluded that adult OHCA victims receiving bystander hands-only CPR have a similar—or in some analyses slightly better—chance of survival compared to conventional CPR, and both are far superior to no CPR (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380).
- A meta-analysis in *Circulation* found dispatcher-assisted chest-compression-only bystander CPR was associated with improved survival compared to standard CPR, reinforcing that any bystander CPR beats none (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/).
- A large observational study found bystander CPR was associated with significantly higher 30-day survival among OHCA patients regardless of etiology, and both CPR types outperformed no bystander CPR after adjustment (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31129226/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/).

Nuances: For pediatric OHCA, evidence is more mixed—some analyses suggest conventional CPR (with ventilation) may outperform compression-only CPR in children, though both still beat no CPR (https://www.resuscitationjournal.com/article/S0300-9572(18)31067-0/pdf). Also, some critiques (e.g., in *The Lancet*) note methodological limitations in meta-analyses possibly overstating compression-only benefits relative to conventional CPR, but this concerns comparisons *between* CPR types, not CPR versus no CPR.

**Conclusion:** The claim is well-supported by the evidence for adults; hands-only CPR clearly improves survival versus no bystander CPR. It is not false.
